Transcript

Welcome to your science briefing for Friday, November 20th. Today we cover a wave of stories where computation is reshaping discovery, from an old mathematician's notebooks to new maps of how the heart burns fuel, plus a major leadership shake-up at a chipmaker central to the AI industry.

We'll start with biotech. The Belgian company Argenx has agreed to acquire Unnatural Products, a biotech that works on oral peptide drugs, in a deal worth up to one point one five billion dollars, according to Endpoints News and Fierce Biotech. Argenx will pay five hundred fifty million dollars upfront, with the rest tied to development and regulatory milestones. Unnatural Products, founded in 2016 by researchers at the University of California, Santa Cruz, builds macrocyclic peptides, a class of molecules that can survive the gut and potentially let drugs that once required injection be taken as pills. According to Fierce Biotech, the company's platform uses AI-guided design along with large-scale synthesis and screening, and it has already partnered with Merck and Novartis. Argenx, known for its antibody drug Vyvgart, says it will keep Unnatural Products' roughly fifty-person team in Santa Cruz as its new hub for this technology. The deal was covered across trade, tech, and science press, six outlets in all, a sign of how closely the industry is watching the shift toward oral peptide drugs as an alternative to injectable biologics.

Next, a closely watched cancer immunotherapy result. Moderna and Merck announced that a personalized messenger RNA vaccine against melanoma, the deadliest form of skin cancer, reduced the risk of death or recurrence by 42 percent compared with standard treatment, according to Ars Technica. This comes from a Phase 3 trial of one thousand one hundred thirty-seven patients with stage two-B through stage four melanoma that had been surgically removed. Patients were randomized, with two-thirds receiving the vaccine combined with Merck's existing antibody drug Keytruda, and the rest receiving Keytruda alone. It's important to note these are top-line results released by the companies themselves, ahead of a scheduled presentation at the European Society for Medical Oncology conference in Madrid; the companies say the full data has been accepted for publication in the New England Journal of Medicine, but that peer-reviewed paper isn't out yet. The story drew over two hundred points and dozens of comments on Hacker News, reflecting strong public interest in personalized cancer vaccines as a treatment category.

Staying with biomedical research, a peer-reviewed paper in Nature revisits a basic assumption about how the heart gets its energy. Researchers at Rutgers and the University of Utah, led by Ahmad Cluntun, studied mouse heart tissue and found that even when a key transporter called the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier is genetically removed, the heart muscle still oxidizes glucose-derived carbon for fuel. The authors report this happens because another transporter, called MCT1, which is normally known for moving lactate across the outer cell membrane, is also present inside mitochondria, the cell's energy-producing structures. Working together with an enzyme called LDHB, MCT1 lets lactate be converted directly into pyruvate and fuel for the cell's electron transport chain, essentially a parallel fuel pathway the authors say runs alongside the one textbooks describe. When they removed MCT1 in mice, the hearts lost metabolic flexibility and were more likely to fail and lead to death after stress from hormonal overactivation or simulated heart attacks. This paper is just three weeks old and has already picked up about a dozen citations, an early signal of interest in a top journal.

In computational biology, a paper in Nature Methods describes a new imaging tool for watching brain activity. Researchers at the McGovern Institute and MIT, led by Zeguan Wang, built a light-sheet microscope that can track voltage changes, not just calcium levels, in neurons spread across much of the brain of larval zebrafish, scanning at over two hundred volumes per second. The authors report they captured voltage signals from roughly a quarter of all neurons in the brain and found that neurons active during different stages of visually evoked brain activity sequences were located in different regions, with stimulus-independent bursts of activity mapping to the cerebellum and medulla. The authors suggest this kind of whole-brain voltage mapping could open new ways to study how neural circuits actually operate. The paper has drawn 24 citations in its first fourteen weeks, solid early uptake for a methods paper.

Now, a mathematics story that generated enormous public interest. According to the Guardian, the Finnish logician Jan von Plato has spent nearly a decade trying to decode sixteen notebooks the mathematician Kurt Gödel wrote in the early 1940s, over a thousand pages written in an obsolete German shorthand. Progress was slow, about a page a week, until von Plato enlisted the AI model Claude in September. Within days, von Plato says, Claude produced a six hundred fifty page digest of the material, which revealed that Gödel had proved hundreds of theorems no one knew about. Von Plato had Claude extract every theorem for which Gödel had a proof, a sketch of one, or an idea for one, finding six hundred sixty-three candidates. Running these through a proof-verification program called Coq, von Plato reports about four hundred were confirmed as stated, roughly two hundred needed minor corrections, and about fifty turned out to be false, which matches notes where Gödel himself had flagged some results as incorrect. Among the findings, von Plato says Claude reconstructed a proof, missing one small step, that Gödel had likely solved a famous problem in set theory decades before it was credited to another mathematician who won the Fields Medal for it. An outside logician at the University of Notre Dame, not involved in the work, said that if the reconstruction holds up, it's historically interesting, though it will take historians to sort out how much credit belongs to Gödel versus the AI. This story is only a week old but drew over four hundred Hacker News points and more than a hundred comments, which is why we're covering it despite its youth.

In a related vein, Science News profiled a brain-computer interface trial through its podcast series. A volunteer named Casey Harrell, who lost his ability to speak due to ALS, has electrode arrays implanted in his brain as part of the BrainGate2 clinical trial. The system reads signals from his speech motor cortex and translates his intended words into speech through a nearby computer, which he says he now uses up to fourteen hours a day. Leigh Hochberg, who directs the BrainGate consortium, cautions that decoding speech specifically is still very early for the field, with only a small number of people worldwide who have used an implanted interface for this purpose. This is a single-source story from Science News, built around interviews rather than new peer-reviewed data, so take the specifics as one patient's experience within an ongoing trial rather than a broad clinical result.

On the infectious disease front, GEN reports on a Nature paper from researchers at Albert Einstein College of Medicine, Institut Pasteur, and LSU Health Shreveport describing, in near-atomic detail, how Andes virus, a hantavirus that can spread person to person, latches onto human cells. Using cryo-electron microscopy combined with an AI-designed protein scaffold to stabilize the viral spike, the team showed that a human receptor called protocadherin-1 binds asymmetrically inside a deep pocket formed by four copies of a viral protein, rather than at a site on a single subunit. The researchers also found that neutralizing antibodies block infection either by obstructing that pocket or by physically blocking the receptor's approach. Because the receptor is long and slender while most antibodies are bulkier, the authors suggest that narrower, elongated engineered molecules might reach deeper into the pocket and offer a new direction for antiviral drug design against Andes virus and related hantaviruses like Sin Nombre virus.

Turning to industry news, Nvidia's chief executive Jensen Huang has resigned, effective immediately, according to Wired and The Verge. The move follows a board investigation, announced on November 8th, into Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, an executive at Nvidia customer Megaspeed who U.S. officials reportedly believe was recruited by China's Ministry of State Security. The New York Times later reported Huang also had a relationship with a direct report at Nvidia, which a source told Wired likely weighed more heavily in the board's decision than the espionage allegations. Huang sent a companywide email acknowledging the affair and apologizing to his family and employees. Nvidia's chief financial officer, Colette Kress, will serve as interim CEO while the board considers internal and external candidates for a permanent replacement. Nvidia's board said it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised, but that its inquiry will examine all available information.

Finally, in physics, a study in Physical Review Letters from researchers at the University of Science and Technology of China used a cold-atom quantum simulator to study a phenomenon related to the Schwinger effect, in which a strong electric field can pull particle-antiparticle pairs directly out of the vacuum. Because this pair production normally requires particles to tunnel over long distances, it's extremely rare and hard to observe directly. By building a tunable analog system using a one-dimensional lattice gauge theory, the authors report they could adjust the background field to favor pair production and directly track the system's evolution over time. They found excitation patterns resembling particle modes seen in a related theoretical model, which they interpret through what they call a string inversion mechanism. The authors say the approach opens a path toward quantum-simulation experiments that can controllably tune particle pair production and study far-from-equilibrium dynamics. The paper is seven weeks old and has already drawn about seventy citations, among the fastest-accumulating results in today's briefing.

That's the briefing for Friday, November 20th. Thanks for listening, and we'll be back tomorrow with more.

Transcript

Welcome to your science briefing for Saturday, November 21st. Today we trace a thread running through biology, mathematics, and artificial intelligence: how computation, whether in cells, in theorems, or in neural networks, is reshaping what we can discover. We'll cover a pivotal gene-editing trial, new insight into how the brain organizes its activity, a cancer mechanism involving cell-to-cell lipid theft, a topological explanation for a famous voting paradox, an AI system that can now predict how DNA variants behave in specific cell types, and the biggest initial public offering in the artificial intelligence industry's short history.

First, biotech. According to Endpoints News and BioPharma Dive, Beam Therapeutics announced that its base-edited therapy for sickle cell disease succeeded in a Phase one, two clinical trial, hitting its primary endpoint. This is a company announcement, not yet an independent peer-reviewed report, but it matters because it points toward a third one-time therapy option for sickle cell disease, a condition that has historically required lifelong management. Both biotech trade outlets covered the news within the same week, underscoring its significance to people tracking the gene-editing field. Details on the exact trial results beyond meeting the goal were not available in this reporting, so we'll be watching for the full data.

Next, to systems neuroscience. A paper in Nature Neuroscience from researchers at Forschungszentrum Julich, the University of Washington, and the Allen Institute asks a basic question: what determines how many independent patterns, or dimensions, of activity the brain's neurons can explore at once? Using high-density recordings called Neuropixels in the mouse cortex, the authors report that brain areas operate in what they call a sensitive regime, where local recurrent synaptic connections, the networks neurons form among themselves, play a strong role in shaping this dimensionality. They found that specific wiring patterns, or network motifs, in these local circuits explained much of the effect, and that these same motifs showed up in a large dataset of synaptic recordings from both mouse and human brains. The authors conclude that local circuitry itself helps set the range of activity patterns available to larger brain networks. This paper has picked up fifty-two citations in the fourteen weeks since publication, a fast pace that reflects strong interest from the systems neuroscience community, though as always, early citations are a sign of attention rather than a final verdict on the work.

Staying in biomedical research, a paper in Nature Cancer from Fox Chase Cancer Center, the French national research agency CNRS, and Inserm describes an unusual way that pancreatic tumors get fed. Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma is a cancer where supporting cells called cancer-associated fibroblasts make up most of the tumor's mass, yet the tumor often lacks functional blood vessels. The authors report that these fibroblasts acquire lipids from the bloodstream and then hand off fragments of their own cell membranes, including cholesterol, directly to cancer cells through a process called trogocytosis, literally nibbling of membrane. They found this depends on a protein called ANO6, which gets activated when cancer cells and fibroblasts form direct contacts that trigger calcium signaling. The same mechanism, the authors report, also helps the fibroblasts suppress the tumor-killing T cells of the immune system. Blocking ANO6 slowed tumor growth in their experiments, partly by cutting off the cholesterol supply, and also reduced immune suppression. This is a cell-based study, with twenty-eight citations in three weeks, a solid early pace, and the authors frame ANO6 as a candidate drug target rather than a proven one.

From a more theoretical angle, a paper in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences from Washington University in Saint Louis, the Santa Fe Institute, and the University of Washington revisits a sixty-five-year-old idea from population geneticist Motoo Kimura, who related the information a population gains through natural selection to a measure of selection's inefficiency called substitution load. The authors report that Kimura's original model doesn't match results from selection experiments in the bacterium Escherichia coli. Borrowing a concept called regret from computational learning theory, a field that studies how algorithms learn under uncertainty, they develop a new way to measure how efficiently selection converts environmental information into genetic information. They validated their bounds experimentally and found that natural selection behaves like what computer scientists would call an asymptotically optimal learning algorithm, meaning it eventually extracts information about the environment about as efficiently as any comparable process could. This is a theoretical and experimental paper with eleven citations in three weeks.

Now for mathematics. Quanta Magazine reports on new work addressing a two-hundred-forty-year-old puzzle first noticed by the French mathematician Nicolas de Condorcet: that majority voting among three or more candidates can produce a circular result, where each candidate loses to another in head-to-head comparison, even though every individual voter has a perfectly consistent ranking. Economist Kenneth Arrow later proved more generally that no voting system can satisfy a few basic fairness conditions simultaneously. According to Quanta, three researchers, building on a nineteen ninety-three model by Yuliy Baryshnikov, have now shown that the space of all possible ballots and their relationships has the shape of a Klein bottle, a surface famous for having no distinct inside or outside. The piece describes how representing each possible ballot as a triangle and gluing matching triangles together produces this shape, and how the paradoxical, circular voting outcomes appear precisely at the twisted seams of that construction. This gives mathematicians a geometric way to think about why fair voting systems run into trouble. The story drew modest attention on Hacker News, with five points and one comment, but was covered by Quanta Magazine specifically because it illustrates how topology can formalize an old problem in social choice theory.

Turning to artificial intelligence applied to genomics, Nature reports that researchers at Google DeepMind in London have released a model called AlphaGenome 2, which predicts how changes in non-coding DNA, the ninety-eight percent of the human genome that doesn't code for proteins, affect gene activity in specific cell types. According to Nature, the team trained the model on single-cell gene activity data from more than one hundred million cells across sixty-eight tissue types, a step up from the earlier AlphaGenome 1, which was trained on bulk, mixed-cell samples and could not say which cell type a given variant would act in. James Lee, an immunologist at the Francis Crick Institute who led a 2024 study identifying a DNA variant linked to inflammatory bowel disease, told Nature that the new model reproduced his team's finding, which had taken a year and a half of laboratory experiments, in about thirty minutes. DeepMind researcher Ziga Avsec said the model can also be given new single-cell data, such as from diseased cells, to generate fresh predictions about disease-linked variants. It's worth noting that a company preprint describing the model has been posted but, per Nature's reporting, is not yet an independent peer-reviewed study. Still, Lee called the overlap with his own hard-won results reassuring.

Finally, in AI industry news, The Verge reports that Anthropic confirmed its initial public offering could value the company as high as one point four trillion dollars, with shares expected to price between seventy and seventy-eight dollars. That's lower than earlier expectations of up to two trillion dollars, according to Reuters, as cited by The Verge, following months of debate over AI safety and what the outlet describes as souring public opinion toward AI companies and their data center investments. For comparison, The Verge notes that rival OpenAI was valued at one point two five trillion dollars as of last week. According to reporting from The Wall Street Journal, cited by The Verge, Anthropic is aiming to begin trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol A-N-T as soon as next week. This would make Anthropic one of the most valuable publicly traded companies in the world, a striking marker of how much capital is now flowing into artificial intelligence.

And a quick note from the Worth Reading file: mathematician Terence Tao wrote on his blog about using coding agents, AI tools that write and modify software, to rebuild an interactive logic-teaching game he calls the Lean Grimoire, named after the Lean proof assistant, a software tool for writing formally verified mathematical proofs. The project reworks a 2018 teaching tool for propositional and first-order logic, now with an option to display an in-progress Lean proof and a lighthearted fantasy-themed mode. Tao is inviting playtesters to help refine it as a teaching tool. The post drew sixty-four points and eleven comments on Hacker News, notable engagement for a blog post about math pedagogy tools.

That's your briefing for today. Across gene therapy, brain circuits, cancer biology, voting theory, genomic AI, and industry finance, the common thread remains computation revealing structure we couldn't see before. Thanks for listening, and we'll be back tomorrow.

Transcript

Welcome to your daily science briefing for Sunday, November 22. Today we move from the business and safety side of obesity drugs, through new tools for reading the genome, to a landmark result in pure mathematics, and we close with how real-world institutions are drawing lines around artificial intelligence.

We start with biotech and pharma. The investment group Blackstone Life Sciences has committed up to one and a half billion dollars to help fund research and development on Pfizer's obesity drug candidate berobenatide, according to reporting from Endpoints News, STAT, and BioPharma Dive. This is a company and investor announcement, not a clinical result, so we don't yet know what the money will buy in terms of trial data. The deal made it into three separate biotech trade outlets, which signals that financing structures like this are becoming a notable feature of the crowded obesity drug space, as companies look for ways to share the cost of expensive late-stage development.

Staying with obesity drugs, the Food and Drug Administration has issued a warning that GLP-1 drugs carry a potential risk for a rare but serious eye condition, according to STAT and Endpoints News. The condition is called non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, sometimes referred to as an eye stroke. It results from insufficient blood flow to the optic nerve, typically causing sudden vision loss, and in severe cases it can lead to blindness. STAT reports there are currently no proven treatments for the condition. The FDA is now requiring drugmakers, including Novo Nordisk, maker of Ozempic and Wegovy, and Eli Lilly, maker of Mounjaro and Zepbound, to update their labels to inform patients and doctors of this risk. STAT notes that side effects like this can surface in real-world use even when they weren't observed in clinical trials, simply because so many more people are now taking these drugs. This is a regulatory action backed by two independent trade outlets, not a single company's claim, which is part of why it matters.

Next, biology and biomedical research. A large international team led by Nelson Johansen and colleagues at the Allen Institute for Brain Science has published, in the journal Cell, a multiomic atlas of the basal ganglia, a set of brain regions involved in motor control, learning, emotion, and cognition. The researchers profiled one point eight million individual cell nuclei from humans, macaques, and marmosets, covering eight basal ganglia structures, and combined measurements of gene expression, open chromatin, and spatial location. By aligning this data across species and against existing mouse and human whole-brain atlases, the authors identified sixty-one cell types that appear to be conserved across these primates over seventy-six million years of evolution. One specific finding: the broad dorsal-to-ventral spatial organization of these brain regions turned out to be more evolutionarily conserved than finer distinctions like receptor type or structural compartment. The authors also mapped genetic risk for psychiatric and neurodegenerative diseases onto specific cell populations within this atlas. This paper has drawn thirty-six citations in the three weeks since publication, suggesting researchers are already treating it as a reference resource for basal ganglia biology.

A much shorter item next. Science dot org published a headline claiming that ancient DNA has confirmed a barbarian tribe's mythic origin story is true. That headline alone generated two hundred sixty-one points and two hundred seventy-two comments on Hacker News, showing strong public interest in the intersection of ancient genomics and history. Unfortunately, our source material for this story is limited to that headline, so we can't tell you which tribe, which myth, or what the genetic evidence actually showed. We'll flag it here as a signal worth watching rather than a reportable finding.

Moving to computational biology. Researchers led by Wenmin Zhang at the Montreal Heart Institute and the University of Montreal have published a new statistical method in Nature Genetics called Robust SparsePro, or RSparsePro, for a technique known as fine-mapping. Fine-mapping is used to narrow down which genetic variants, out of many that are statistically associated with a trait or disease in a genome-wide association study, are most likely to be the actual causal ones. This process typically relies on a reference panel that approximates the correlation structure between nearby genetic variants, called linkage disequilibrium, but mismatches between that reference panel and the actual study population can distort the results. The authors report that in simulation studies with varying degrees of this mismatch, their method consistently achieved higher power and accuracy than existing approaches. When applied to real data on protein levels in blood and on complex disease risk, the authors say RSparsePro identified variant sets more enriched for likely functional effects, with better replication across independent studies and reference panels. They also report the method flagged biologically relevant variants in drug target genes and offered potential regulatory insights related to LDL cholesterol. The paper has drawn eleven citations in three weeks, a methods paper finding early traction in the genomics community.

Now to mathematics, for a result that moves on a much longer timescale. Zhenhua Liu, at Princeton University, has published a paper in the Annals of Mathematics that settles a long-standing conjecture by Frederick Almgren concerning area-minimizing submanifolds, geometric objects that minimize surface area subject to constraints, somewhat like soap films. Almgren had conjectured that such minimizing submanifolds could have singular sets, points or regions where the smooth structure breaks down, with a fractal character. Liu constructs examples confirming this, and the author states the result is sharp in terms of dimension, meaning it can't be improved. The paper also shows these constructions can be made to match arbitrarily prescribed patterns in what's called the Almgren stratification, a way of organizing how singularities are structured, and that the results hold across several different mathematical frameworks used to study these objects. This paper has accumulated sixteen citations in three weeks, modest in absolute terms but notable for a pure mathematics result of this nature, where recognition often builds slowly.

Next, AI for biology and medicine. Google DeepMind has released a new AI model called AlphaGenome 2, as reported by The Verge. It is the successor to last year's AlphaGenome and is designed to predict how DNA variants affect gene activity in specific types and states of cells, rather than giving one general prediction for the whole body. According to the company, the same genetic variant can have very different effects depending on which cell type it's acting in, and AlphaGenome 2 was trained on more than one hundred million individual cell profiles spanning sixty-eight tissues to capture that variation. Google says the model identifies nearly twice as many variants that can change gene expression compared with its previous leading model, and that it can make predictions about new cell types or states it wasn't specifically trained on. DeepMind researcher Adam Gayoso told The Verge the significance lies in, quote, tying human genetics to cell biology, end quote, while genomics lead Žiga Avsec said this cell-level detail matters because drug development targets specific proteins in specific cell types. Avsec also noted the model is more computationally expensive to run than its predecessor, which is why DeepMind isn't replacing the earlier, broader model with it just yet. Google is making AlphaGenome 2 available for non-commercial research now, with limited commercial preview access. It's worth remembering this is a company announcement amplified by one tech outlet, so independent scientific evaluation of its real-world predictive accuracy is still to come.

Finally, a story about AI hitting a very concrete boundary. United Airlines announced this week that it is banning AI agents from making flight reservations on behalf of travelers, according to CBS News. The airline said that letting personal AI assistants handle bookings could expose sensitive account information and lead to unintended purchases, account changes, or misuse of frequent-flyer miles. United also said using an AI agent for tasks like checking in could violate federal regulations that require travelers to personally verify their luggage doesn't contain banned substances. The airline is updating its policies to block access to such agents both directly on its own platforms and indirectly through travel agencies and aggregators. Aviation analyst Henry Harteveldt told CBS News that United is essentially trying to avoid adding another costly intermediary on top of existing ones like search engines and price-comparison sites, since flight searches cost airlines money. Notably, other carriers are taking a different approach. Southwest, for instance, has made its flight inventory viewable directly through ChatGPT. This story drew six hundred eighty-three points and over seven hundred comments on Hacker News, reflecting broad public interest in how companies are setting limits on autonomous AI agents acting on people's behalf.

That's today's briefing. Thanks for listening, and we'll be back tomorrow with more.

Transcript

Welcome to your science briefing for Monday, November 23rd. Today we're checking what's actually been validated this week, from a major public health setback and a first-in-class drug approval, to vetted advances in brain mapping, genomics, AI diagnostics, mathematics, and physics simulation.

We start with the biggest public health story. The Pan American Health Organization has announced that the United States has lost its measles elimination status, a designation it held for twenty-six years. According to Nature and NPR, the loss follows an outbreak that has caused more than five thousand seven hundred infections and ten deaths this year, the deadliest measles episode in the US in more than three decades. The organization strips elimination status when one genetic variant of the virus has circulated continuously for twelve months or more, which genetic data confirmed was happening here. Mexico and Bolivia also lost their status. NPR reports that across the Americas, confirmed measles cases this year reached over fifty-eight thousand, compared with about twelve thousand six hundred during the same period last year. Virologist Paul Offit, of Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, told Nature that falling vaccination rates left parts of the population susceptible. NPR adds that nationwide kindergarten vaccination rates have dropped to about ninety-two point four percent, below the ninety-five percent threshold needed to prevent outbreaks. Unusually, around forty percent of US cases this year were in adults twenty and older, a shift Offit attributes to generations who were never naturally infected and, in some cases, never vaccinated. Physicians are also seeing a rare phenomenon, congenital measles, with six cases reported in Pennsylvania alone this year. This story made the cut because it was covered by seven outlets across science press, general press, and health trade press, reflecting its consequence for public health policy and practice.

Next, a genuine regulatory milestone. The Food and Drug Administration has approved Bayer's drug Sunharbo to reduce the recurrence of stroke, according to STAT. It's the first approved medication in a new class that inhibits a clotting protein called factor XIa, a mechanism thought to prevent harmful clots without raising bleeding risk the way many existing blood thinners do. STAT reports that in a Phase 3 trial of people who'd already had a stroke, eight point four percent of those on placebo had a second stroke, compared with six point two percent on Sunharbo, a twenty-six percent relative risk reduction. Put another way, fifty-three patients would need to be treated for a year to prevent one recurrent stroke. Endpoints News and BioPharma Dive both covered the approval as well, which is why it earns a spot here, three trade outlets reporting on a clinical trial result with a clear, first-in-class mechanism.

Moving to neuroscience, researchers at the Allen Institute for Brain Science have published, in the journal Cell, a cellular-resolution spatial transcriptomics atlas of the basal ganglia in humans, rhesus macaques, and common marmosets. The authors sampled more than one million cells in each species and combined spatial data with a single-cell RNA sequencing taxonomy to map molecular organization across these subcortical structures, which are involved in movement and implicated in neurodegenerative disorders. They report stereotyped gene expression gradients across the striatum and describe a core-shell organization within part of the globus pallidus they hadn't previously resolved at this detail. The authors call it a foundational resource for future work on basal ganglia health and disease. It's drawn seventeen citations in three weeks, a sign the field is already building on it.

In global health research, a Global Burden of Disease study published in Nature Medicine estimates cervical cancer's worldwide toll and forecasts it to 2050. The authors, affiliated with the University of Washington's Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation, estimate eight hundred eighty-seven thousand new cases and three hundred sixty-nine thousand deaths globally in 2023. They found incidence and mortality rates more than four and seven times higher, respectively, in low-income countries compared with high-income ones. While age-standardized rates are projected to decline somewhat by 2050, the authors forecast absolute case counts to rise by about twenty percent and deaths by nearly forty percent, driven by population growth and aging. They attribute essentially all of this burden to human papillomavirus infection, with tobacco use contributing about six percent globally. This paper has also picked up seventeen citations in three weeks, flagging it as a policy-relevant benchmark for tracking progress against a highly preventable cancer.

On the tools side of biology, researchers primarily from the Broad Institute and the University of Helsinki, writing in Nature Genetics, describe a new statistical method called SAIGE-QTL for mapping how genetic variants affect gene expression at single-cell resolution. Existing approaches either average expression across cells, losing resolution, or use models poorly suited to the count-based nature of single-cell data. The authors report that their Poisson mixed-model approach scales to large datasets while properly accounting for different numbers of cells per donor. In a test on one point two million immune cells, it identified nearly forty-nine percent more genes with significant expression associations than conventional pseudobulk analysis, and the authors say it also enables new kinds of rare-variant and long-range genetic testing. The method has already accumulated twenty-six citations in three weeks, suggesting quick uptake by geneticists working with single-cell data.

In mathematics, a paper in the Annals of Mathematics, from researchers at University College London and Humboldt University of Berlin, proves the finiteness part of the Gopakumar-Vafa conjecture, a longstanding question connecting string theory and enumerative geometry. The conjecture predicts that certain invariants describing six-dimensional symplectic spaces are whole numbers and that almost all of them equal zero. The integer part was proved years ago by other mathematicians; this paper supplies the finiteness proof, using a modified version of earlier cluster techniques combined with results from geometric measure theory. It's accumulated thirty-eight citations in three weeks, reflecting significant interest from mathematicians and physicists in a proof that closes out a conjecture dating back decades.

In applied AI for medicine, The Lancet published a prospective feasibility study, led by researchers at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Google, testing a conversational diagnostic AI system in real ambulatory primary care settings. Beyond the headline and the fact that it's a peer-reviewed feasibility study, our source material doesn't include further detail on methods or results, so we'll leave it there, noting only that it has drawn twenty-four citations in eight weeks, suggesting active interest in moving conversational AI diagnostics from lab settings into live clinical practice.

On the frontier AI front, OpenAI announced two new models last week, GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol, according to the company's own announcement. Astra is pitched as the flagship model for complex professional work, while Sol is a cheaper, faster model for everyday tasks. OpenAI says Astra scored five point two points higher than its predecessor on a benchmark testing multistep professional work, called Agents' Last Exam, while costing less than a third as much to run. The company also claims Astra sets a new high on a science-focused benchmark called the Vals Science Index, which tests interpreting biological data and running simulated experiments. These are the company's own benchmark claims, not independent verification. The release drew well over thirteen hundred points and more than eight hundred comments on Hacker News, a signal of substantial developer interest, which is why we're flagging it despite it being company-reported rather than independently assessed.

Finally, in physics, a paper in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, from researchers at Caltech, the University of Augsburg, and the Flatiron Institute, introduces a neural-network-based method for simulating strongly interacting fermions, systems relevant to understanding unconventional superconductivity. The authors extend an existing neural quantum state technique into a mathematical structure called a Pfaffian, which naturally represents superconducting pairing, calling their method the hidden fermion Pfaffian state. In numerical tests on standard model systems known as Hubbard models, they report state-of-the-art accuracy for both attractive and repulsive interaction regimes, and say the method can capture phases with and without electron pairing while scaling more favorably to larger systems than prior approaches. The paper has drawn forty-seven citations in about thirteen weeks, a strong early signal in the computational physics community.

That's the briefing for today. These are early signals from the past weeks of research, not final verdicts, so keep an eye on how they hold up as more scrutiny arrives. Thanks for listening, and we'll be back tomorrow.

Transcript

Welcome to your daily science briefing for Tuesday, November 24. Today we're covering a CRISPR gene therapy nearing approval, cancer and aging research, a major results in pure mathematics and quantum computing, and the latest frontier AI model from Google.

We start in biotech and pharma. According to Nature, a CRISPR-based gene therapy is poised to receive its first-ever approval from the Food and Drug Administration. Nature's report builds on years of progress in editing genes directly inside the body, though the available text is limited to the headline and a reference to a New England Journal of Medicine paper from earlier this year. This story is about two weeks old and was covered by one outlet so far, with some discussion on Hacker News, so take it as a signal to watch for the formal approval decision rather than a confirmed result.

Next, a clinical trial result from STAT, reported from a major oncology meeting in Madrid. Merck and China's Kelun-Biotech presented randomized Phase 3 results showing their antibody-drug conjugate, called sacituzumab tirumotecan, cut the risk of death by one-third in patients with advanced endometrial cancer, compared with the control arm. STAT notes the drug has already shown survival benefits across multiple cancer types in Kelun's studies in China, where it's approved. Merck is running eighteen global Phase 3 trials of the drug, including ten in women's cancers, as it works toward approvals outside China. STAT frames this partly in business terms too: the drug is central to Merck's plan to offset revenue it will lose when its immunotherapy Keytruda loses patent protection in 2028. This is a single trade-press report of presented data, not yet a published peer-reviewed paper.

Moving to biology and biomedical research, Nature reports on a newly identified protein that appears to drive aging independent of inflammation. The underlying work, published in the journal Immunity and led by Kannangara and colleagues, was covered briefly by Nature, and the topic drew substantial attention on Hacker News, with 259 points and nearly a hundred comments. The source material available here is limited to a short notice rather than full study details, so we can say only that the finding points to a mechanism for aging that doesn't rely on the inflammatory pathways usually implicated, and it clearly struck a nerve with readers. Full specifics of how the protein was identified and tested await more detailed reporting.

A more detailed peer-reviewed finding comes from Nature Genetics. Researchers led by Lotte Brückner at Germany's Max Delbrück Center, Charité, and the German Cancer Research Center studied extrachromosomal DNA, or ecDNA, a form of cancer genome instability that lets tumor cells amplify oncogenes outside the normal chromosomes. The team found that when ecDNA is damaged, especially under replication stress, it tends to end up misplaced into structures called micronuclei during cell division. Using single-micronucleus sequencing, they showed multiple distinct ecDNA pieces can coalesce inside one micronucleus. Cells that inherit these ecDNA-containing micronuclei showed reduced proliferation and were more likely to die. In patients with MYCN-amplified neuroblastoma, the authors report that a higher frequency of these ecDNA-containing micronuclei at diagnosis was associated with better overall survival. In other words, the very instability that drives tumor growth can also become a liability for cancer cells. This paper is about six weeks old and has already picked up eleven citations, a modest but notable early uptake.

In computational biology, a Nature Methods paper from Jieran Sun and colleagues at the Centre Hospitalier Universitaire Vaudois and the Berlin Institute of Health addresses a practical problem in spatial transcriptomics: how to cluster tissue data into meaningful anatomical regions. The authors built a framework called SACCELERATOR to standardize how these clustering methods are tested. They report that existing benchmarks have been too narrowly focused on one sequencing platform and brain tissue, and that manual annotations often treated as ground truth are themselves biased and error-prone. Rather than simply ranking methods against each other, the authors propose a consensus-based workflow that flags regions where methods disagree, so tissue experts can weigh in directly. Applied to brain and cancer datasets, they say this approach revealed biologically meaningful patterns that individual methods and manual labels had missed. The paper is about thirteen weeks old with twelve citations so far.

Now to mathematics. In the Duke Mathematical Journal, David Gabai and colleagues at Princeton report a proof of a long-standing conjecture by Gordon concerning hyperbolic three-manifolds. They show that the figure-eight knot complement is the unique cusped hyperbolic three-manifold with more than eight non-hyperbolic fillings on a single cusp. They also establish that three is the smallest possible volume for what's called a maximal cusp of a complete hyperbolic three-manifold, a bound achieved exactly by the figure-eight knot complement and a related manifold called its sister. To get there, the authors introduce a new theory involving what they call necklaces of horoballs, which lets them classify manifolds with small cusp volumes and apply existing theorems on filling and drilling these spaces. This is a technical result in low-dimensional topology, published about three weeks ago, already cited nineteen times, a fast pace for a specialized mathematics paper.

In AI for biology and medicine, Flagship Pioneering, the venture firm behind companies like Moderna, announced it is merging three of its biotech startups, Etiome, Cellarity, and Empress Therapeutics, into a single new company called Etcelera. According to the companies, the combined entity will use artificial intelligence to better predict how new medicines will perform in humans before they reach the clinic. This is a company announcement, not an independent study, and was covered by three biotech trade outlets, Endpoints News, Fierce Biotech, and BioPharma Dive, which signals real industry interest even though the predictive claims themselves haven't been independently verified. In related news from the same reporting cycle, Fierce Biotech reported that Geron halted a Phase 3 trial of its drug Rytelo in myelofibrosis after an independent monitoring committee found it was unlikely to show a survival benefit, a reminder that not every late-stage oncology bet pays off even as the industry leans further into predictive AI tools upstream.

In general AI, Google this week introduced Gemini 4 Neon, its newest frontier model, according to the company's own blog post. Google says Neon ranks third overall on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index and second on the Vals Index, and highlights strong scores on benchmarks covering legal research, tax analysis, scientific reasoning, and software engineering. The company reports the model achieved a forty-times reduction in a chemistry-adjacent error metric is not mentioned here, but it does report pricing of three dollars per million input tokens and fifteen dollars per million output tokens, with a one-million-token context window. Google also says Neon produces more secure code than its predecessor, Carbon, on cybersecurity benchmarks, and that internal testing shows improvements in reducing fabricated outputs. All of these figures come from Google's own announcement and benchmark partners it cites, not independent replication. Still, the release generated enormous attention, over a thousand points and more than seven hundred comments on Hacker News, making it one of the most discussed AI stories of the past week.

Finally, in physics, a Science paper from Emma Rosenfeld and colleagues at Google reports progress toward practical fault-tolerant quantum computing. The team experimentally demonstrated a technique called magic state cultivation on a superconducting quantum processor, an alternative to the more resource-intensive process of distillation needed to implement certain quantum logic gates. By implementing cultivation and switching into what's called a surface code, along with a new fault-tolerant measurement protocol, the authors report reducing errors by a factor of forty, achieving a state fidelity of at least point nine nine nine nine, while retaining eight percent of attempts. The authors describe this as an experimental validation that magic state cultivation is a viable path forward for one of quantum computing's central challenges. The paper is six weeks old and has already drawn seventy-five citations, a rapid uptake reflecting strong interest in practical routes to fault tolerance.

That's your briefing for today. Thanks for listening, and we'll be back tomorrow with more.
